concepts.title: Index Numbers: Barometers of Economic Activity
concepts.definition: An index number is a statistical device for measuring changes in a variable -- or a group of related variables -- over time or place, expressed relative to a base period taken as 100. Called the barometers of economic activity, index numbers gauge price levels, industrial output and business conditions at a glance.
concepts.key_idea: One number, one base of 100 -- the index turns sprawling changes into a single readable dial.
concepts.textbook_ref: kest107.txt introduction (index numbers, base period, barometers of economic activity, uses of index numbers)

solution_steps.explain: An index number expresses the level of a variable in one period as a percentage of its level in the base period.
The base period, set at 100, is the reference from which change is measured.
An index of 125 means a 25 percent rise over base -- instant readability for prices, output or trade.

concepts.title: Price Index: Simple and Weighted Averages
concepts.definition: A simple price index compares a commodity's current price with its base price; aggregate and average-of-relatives methods extend this to many commodities. Weighted index numbers attach importance weights -- typically quantities -- so that items bought in bulk move the index more than rare ones.
concepts.key_idea: Current over base times 100 -- the price index is a ratio dressed as a percentage.
concepts.textbook_ref: kest107.txt price index sections (simple index, aggregate method, average of price relatives, weighted index, laspeyres paasche mentions)

solution_steps.explain: Divide the current year's price by the base year's price.
Multiply the ratio by 100 to express it as an index number.

concepts.title: Consumer Price Index and Inflation Measurement
concepts.definition: The consumer price index tracks the retail prices of a basket of goods and services bought by a typical family, revealing changes in the cost of living; wholesale and industrial-production indices serve other sectors. Real income is nominal income deflated by the price index -- the index that links money to its true worth.
concepts.key_idea: The CPI is the cost-of-living dial -- divide money income by the index to know real worth.

solution_steps.explain: Select the goods and services a typical consumer family buys, with their quantities as weights.
Compare the basket's total cost in the current period with its cost in the base period, scaled to 100.
Dividing money income by the price index yields real income -- purchasing power stripped of inflation.
